questions.q: A billing service and an analytics service both subscribe to the `orders` topic, in different consumer groups. The billing service reads and processes an order event. What happens to that event in the topic?

options.t: It stays in the topic until retention removes it; analytics can still read it
It is deleted once billing commits its offset, so the analytics group never receives it
options.why: Kafka does not delete events when they are consumed; reading only moves the reader's own position.

options.t: It is moved to a per-group copy of the topic for billing only
options.why: There is one log per partition; groups track their own offsets in it, nothing is copied per group.

options.t: It is hidden from other groups until billing's transaction commits
options.why: Visibility to other readers is not tied to another group consuming the event; transactions concern the producer's writes.

questions.explain: Events are not deleted when consumed. How long Kafka keeps them is a per-topic retention setting, and every group reads the same log at its own pace.

questions.q: Which of these does a Kafka record carry, according to the Apache Kafka documentation? (Pick the complete list.)

options.t: A key and a value only
options.why: A record also has a timestamp, and may carry headers.

options.t: A value, a schema ID and a checksum chosen by the application
options.why: A schema ID is a Schema Registry convention inside the value bytes, not a field of every record.

options.t: A key, a value, a timestamp and optional headers
A topic name, a partition number and a value; keys are stored separately
options.why: The key is part of the record; the topic and partition are where it is stored.

questions.explain: An event (record, message) has a key, a value, a timestamp and optional headers.

questions.q: A producer sends every event for customer `c-42` with the key `c-42`, to a topic with 6 partitions that never changes. What does Kafka guarantee about those events?

options.t: They are spread over all 6 partitions to balance the load evenly
options.why: Spreading happens for records without a key; with a key, the key decides the partition.

options.t: They are delivered to every consumer in the group
options.why: Within a group, each partition goes to exactly one consumer, so not every consumer sees them.

options.t: They are ordered by timestamp across the whole topic
options.why: Kafka orders records within a partition, not across a topic, and by write order, not timestamp.

options.t: They all go to one partition and are read in the order written

questions.explain: The default partitioner hashes the key to choose a partition, so events with the same key go to the same partition, and a partition is read in the order it was written.

questions.q: A topic `payments` has 4 partitions and is keyed by account ID. The team runs `kafka-topics --alter --partitions 8`. Which statements describe what follows?

options.t: Some account IDs can now hash to a different partition, so ordering for an existing key can be broken across the change
Kafka moves existing records to their new partitions so each key's history stays together
options.why: Existing data is not redistributed when partitions are added.

options.t: A consumer group with auto.offset.reset=latest can miss records written to the new partitions before it notices them
The change is refused because a keyed topic cannot gain partitions
options.why: Partitions can be added to any topic; it is reducing them that is impossible.

options.t: The new partitions are invisible to producers until the brokers restart
options.why: Clients see new partitions after a metadata refresh, not a broker restart.

questions.explain: The docs list the side effects of adding partitions: keys hashed by `hash(key) % partitions` can move, existing data is not redistributed, and consumers using `latest` can miss early records in new partitions.

questions.q: A topic was created with 24 partitions and now holds very little traffic. Can the team reduce it to 6 partitions?

options.t: Yes, with `kafka-topics --alter --partitions 6`
options.why: The tool can only increase the count.

options.t: No. Create a new topic with 6 partitions and move to it
Yes, but only while no consumer group is active
options.why: Group activity is irrelevant: the partition count can't go down at all.

options.t: Yes, but only while no consumer group is reading the topic
options.why: Retention is per topic and does not remove partitions.

questions.explain: The docs state that Kafka cannot reduce the number of partitions of a topic. Choose the count with care, because only adding is possible.

questions.q: A topic has 6 partitions. A consumer group runs 8 consumer instances using the classic protocol. What happens?

options.t: Each consumer reads 6/8 of a partition
options.why: A partition is never split between consumers of one group.

options.t: Kafka adds 2 partitions automatically so every consumer gets one
options.why: Kafka never changes a topic's partition count by itself.

options.t: Two consumers are rejected from the group
options.why: They join the group; they simply get no partitions.

options.t: Six consumers get one partition each and two sit idle

questions.explain: Each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in a group, so the partition count is the maximum parallelism of a group. Extra consumers stay idle until a rebalance gives them partitions.

questions.q: A consumer has processed the record at offset 41 of a partition and commits manually. Which offset should it commit so that a restarted consumer resumes at the right place?

options.why: Committing 41 would make the restarted consumer read offset 41 again.
That would re-read two records.

options.t: Whatever the log-end offset is at commit time
options.why: That would skip every record between 42 and the log end that has not been processed.

questions.explain: The committed offset should always be the offset of the next message the application will read: the last processed offset plus one.

questions.q: A brand-new consumer group with default settings subscribes to a topic that already holds a week of data. Where does it start reading?

options.t: At the earliest offset, replaying the whole week
options.why: That needs auto.offset.reset=earliest; the default is latest.

options.t: At the end of each partition: only new records
It fails with NoOffsetForPartitionException
options.why: That is the behaviour of auto.offset.reset=none, not the default.

options.t: At the offset the last group to read the topic had committed
options.why: Committed offsets belong to one group; a new group has none.

questions.explain: When a group has no committed offset, `auto.offset.reset` decides, and its default is `latest`: start at the end of each partition.

questions.q: A topic has `cleanup.policy=delete`, `retention.ms=604800000` and `retention.bytes=1073741824`. It has 10 partitions. Roughly how much disk can the topic's data occupy (one replica) before size-based retention starts deleting?

options.t: 1 GiB in total, shared by all partitions
options.why: retention.bytes is a per-partition limit, not a topic total.

options.t: Unlimited, because retention.ms takes precedence
options.why: Both limits apply; whichever is reached first triggers deletion.

options.t: 100 MiB, one tenth per partition
options.why: The limit is applied to each partition in full, not divided.

options.t: About 10 GiB: the 1 GiB limit applies to each partition

questions.explain: `retention.bytes` is the maximum size per partition, so multiply it by the number of partitions to get the topic's size.

questions.q: A low-traffic topic has `retention.ms` of 1 hour but keeps data for days. Its `segment.bytes` and `segment.ms` are at their defaults. What explains it?

options.t: Retention deletes whole segments, and the active segment hasn't rolled yet
retention.ms is ignored on topics with fewer than 1 GiB of data
options.why: There is no size threshold for time retention; the issue is how segments roll.

options.t: Retention only runs when a consumer group is empty
options.why: Retention is unrelated to consumer groups.

options.t: The broker's log.retention.hours overrides the topic's retention.ms setting
options.why: A topic-level setting overrides the broker default, not the other way round.

questions.explain: Retention and cleaning work a file at a time. Records in the segment still being written are not deleted until it rolls, at `segment.bytes` (1 GiB) or `segment.ms` (7 days) by default.

questions.q: Which topic is the best fit for `cleanup.policy=compact`?

options.t: A click-stream in which every click is an independent event to count
options.why: Compaction drops older values per key; independent events would be lost.

options.t: An audit log that must keep every change for seven years
options.why: Compaction removes superseded records, the opposite of keeping every change.

options.t: The latest address per customer ID, used to rebuild a cache
A topic whose records have no key
options.why: Compaction keeps the latest value per key; records need keys.

questions.explain: Compaction keeps at least the last value for each key. It suits changelogs of keyed, mutable data, such as reloading a cache or restoring state, not standalone events.

questions.q: On a compacted topic, a producer writes key `user-7` with a null value. What is that record, and what does it do?

options.t: An invalid record: brokers reject null values on compacted topics
options.why: Null values are allowed; they have a special meaning.

options.t: A tombstone: it deletes earlier records with that key
A marker that pauses compaction for that key
options.why: It does the opposite: it lets compaction remove the key.

options.t: A record that resets the key's offset to 0
options.why: Offsets never change in a compacted log.

questions.explain: A keyed record with a null value is a tombstone. It deletes earlier records for its key, and is removed itself once `delete.retention.ms` has passed.

questions.q: Which statements about a compacted topic are true?

options.t: Compaction can change the offset of a record that survives
options.why: Offsets never change; a compacted-away offset is still a valid position.

options.t: The order of the records that remain is never changed
A consumer that reads from the start sees at least the final value of every key
Compaction blocks reads on a partition while it runs
options.why: The cleaner recopies segments in the background and does not block reads.

options.t: Compaction keeps exactly one record per key at all times
options.why: It guarantees at least the last value; the uncompacted head can hold several.

questions.explain: Compaction removes some records but never reorders them, never changes an offset, and a reader from the start always sees at least the last value of every key.

questions.q: What is the unit of replication in Kafka?

options.t: The partition: each has one leader and zero or more followers
The topic: each topic is copied to every broker
options.why: Replication is per partition, with a chosen replication factor, not to every broker.

options.t: The broker: each broker has a standby broker
options.why: Brokers don't pair up; partitions are replicated across brokers.

options.t: The record batch, copied by the producer to several brokers
options.why: The producer writes to the leader only; followers copy from it.

questions.explain: The partition is the unit of replication. All writes go to the leader; followers fetch from it like consumers.

questions.q: A follower replica stops fetching from its leader because its broker is overloaded. What removes it from the in-sync replica set (ISR)?

options.t: The producer, when its next acks=all write to that partition times out
options.why: Producers don't manage the ISR; the leader does.

options.t: Nothing: a replica stays in the ISR for its lifetime
options.why: The ISR changes all the time as replicas fall behind and catch up.

options.t: The consumer group coordinator
options.why: The group coordinator manages consumer groups, not replicas.

options.t: The leader, after replica.lag.time.max.ms (30 s by default)

questions.explain: The leader tracks the ISR and removes a follower that hasn't fetched, or hasn't caught up to the log end, for `replica.lag.time.max.ms`.

questions.q: When does a record written to a partition become visible to consumers?

options.t: As soon as the leader writes it to its own log, whatever the producer's acks
options.why: Consumers only get committed records, not merely written ones.

options.t: When it is on all in-sync replicas, whatever acks was used
Only if the producer used acks=all
options.why: Visibility doesn't depend on the producer's acks setting.

options.t: After the next segment roll
options.why: Segments roll for retention; visibility doesn't wait for them.

questions.explain: Only committed messages are given to consumers: a record becomes visible when it is on all in-sync replicas, whatever `acks` the producer used.

questions.q: Which setup does the Apache Kafka documentation give as a typical durable configuration?

options.t: Replication factor 2, min.insync.replicas 2, acks=1
options.why: acks=1 doesn't wait for followers, so min.insync.replicas has no effect.

options.t: Replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas 3, acks=all
options.why: With min ISR equal to the replication factor, one broker down stops all writes.

options.t: Replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas 2, acks=all
Replication factor 1, min.insync.replicas 1, acks=all
options.why: One copy can't survive a broker loss.

questions.explain: The docs' durability example: create the topic with replication factor 3, set `min.insync.replicas` to 2 and produce with `acks=all`, so a majority of replicas must have a write before it is acknowledged.

questions.q: A topic has replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas=1`. Two followers fall out of the ISR. A producer with `acks=all` sends a record. What happens?

options.t: It is refused with NotEnoughReplicasException, since two replicas are missing
options.why: That happens only when the ISR is smaller than min.insync.replicas, here 1.

options.t: The write blocks until both followers rejoin
options.why: acks=all waits for the current ISR, not for every assigned replica.

options.t: The producer silently falls back to acks=1
options.why: Producers don't change acks by themselves.

options.t: It succeeds, stored on the leader only

questions.explain: `acks=all` means the current ISR, not all assigned replicas. With the ISR shrunk to the leader and `min.insync.replicas=1`, the write succeeds with one copy and is lost if that broker fails.

questions.q: What does setting `unclean.leader.election.enable=true` trade?

options.t: Durability for availability: an out-of-sync replica may lead and lose data
Latency for throughput: leaders are elected in batches
options.why: Batched elections happen anyway; this setting is about which replicas may lead.

options.t: Nothing, because Kafka never elects a replica outside the ISR
options.why: That is the default behaviour; this setting turns it off.

options.t: Availability for durability: partitions stay offline until every replica returns
options.why: That is the default (false); true does the reverse.

questions.explain: When every in-sync replica is down, the default is to wait for one of them (consistent, maybe unavailable). Unclean election lets the first replica back lead (available, may lose committed messages).

questions.q: Kafka's ISR model tolerates f replica failures without losing committed data with how many replicas, compared with a majority-quorum system?

options.t: 2f+1, the same as a majority quorum
options.why: That is the majority-quorum figure; the ISR model needs fewer.

options.t: f+1, because only ISR members can be elected and a write commits only when all of them have it
f, because the controller keeps an extra copy
options.why: The controller stores metadata, not partition data.

options.t: 2f, because each replica has a standby
options.why: There are no per-replica standbys.

questions.explain: A majority quorum needs 2f+1 replicas to survive f failures. Kafka's ISR needs only f+1, because a write commits only when every ISR member has it and only ISR members can be elected.

questions.q: In Apache Kafka 4.x, where is the cluster's metadata (topics, partitions, leaders, configuration) managed?

options.t: In a ZooKeeper ensemble the brokers connect to
options.why: Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper mode; 4.x supports only KRaft.

options.t: In each producer's local cache, synchronised by gossip
options.why: Clients cache metadata they fetch from brokers; they don't own it.

options.t: A quorum of KRaft controllers
In the __consumer_offsets topic
options.why: That topic stores consumer group offsets, not cluster metadata.

questions.explain: Since Kafka 4.0 metadata is managed by KRaft: controllers form the metadata quorum, with one active controller and the others as hot standbys.

questions.q: A KRaft cluster runs 3 controllers. How many controller failures can the metadata quorum survive and keep working?

options.t: None
options.why: A majority (2 of 3) remains after one failure.

options.t: Two
options.why: With two down, 1 of 3 is not a majority.

options.t: Three, because brokers take over
options.why: Brokers don't take over the controller role.

options.t: One, because a majority must stay alive

questions.explain: A majority of controllers must be alive: 3 controllers tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2.

questions.q: Why do Kafka consumers pull data from brokers rather than having brokers push it?

options.t: Push is not possible over TCP
options.why: Push is possible; Kafka chose pull for its trade-offs.

options.t: A slow consumer can fall behind and catch up, and brokers can batch
Pull is required for exactly-once semantics
options.why: Exactly-once relies on idempotence and transactions, not on pull.

options.t: Pull guarantees lower latency than push in every case, which streaming needs
options.why: The docs don't claim that; long polls avoid busy-waiting, but latency is not the reason.

questions.explain: With pull, a consumer slower than production simply falls behind and catches up, and the broker can batch aggressively. Push tends to overwhelm a slow consumer.
